list.listitem: Bariatric surgery is an option for patients with a body mass index (BMI) greater than 40 or BMI greater than 35 in the presence of significant comorbidities. C
Bariatric surgical procedures produce more substantial weight loss in morbidly obese patients than conventional behavioral programs A and can reduce all-cause mortality. B

The roux-en-Y gastric bypass and the adjustable gastric banding are the most common surgical procedures; together they have a postoperative mortality rate of 1% and a rate of serious complications of 10%. C
Potential candidates for bariatric surgery should undergo preoperative evaluation by a team of medical, surgical, psychological, and nutritional professionals. C

background.definition: Bariatric surgical procedures reduce calorie intake and/or calorie absorption by providing anatomical changes in the gastrointestinal tract. See for descriptions of the surgical procedures.

list.listitem: There were over 100,000 bariatric surgical procedures performed in 2003.
Overweight (BMI >25 kg/m2) and obesity (BMI >30 kg/m2) affect 67% of the United States population.
Morbid obesity (BMI >40 kg/m2) affects 5% of the population.
Over $117 billion dollars is spent annually treating obesity and obesity-related comorbidities.
Obesity is a multifactorial disease involving behavioral, societal, and genetic components.

Modern day lifestyle involving the excess consumption of calorie-dense, processed foods and the use of automation (eg, automobiles, elevators, remote controls) to replace physical activity are contributors to the current obesity epidemic.
Certain medical conditions (eg, hypercortisolism, hypothyroidism) and certain medications (eg, beta-blockers, thiazolidinediones) lead to weight gain and may contribute to obesity.
Children with one obese parent have a 40% chance of developing obesity in adulthood while those with two obese parents have an 80% chance.
Rarely, single gene defect syndromes including leptin deficiency, leptin-receptor deficiency, and Prader-Willi syndrome are the cause of an individual's morbid obesity.

Pathologic consequences of morbid obesity include coronary artery disease, diabetes mellitus, obstructive sleep apnea, debilitating arthritis, obstructive and restrictive lung disease, and various forms of cancer.
Other medical conditions associated with obesity include metabolic syndrome, polycystic ovary syndrome, Cushing's disease, and hypogonadism.
Certain psychiatric conditions including binge eating disorder, major depression, and body dysmorphic disorder are common among obese individuals.
The BMI is a reliable tool in screening patients who are at increased risk for morbidity and mortality due to obesity and who may be candidates for bariatric surgery. B

Maintaining an energy-balanced diet and an active lifestyle are helpful in sustaining a healthy weight and preventing weight regain. Utilizing portion-controlled meals and meal replacements can assist in controlling daily calorie intake. A
Children should be encouraged to engage in at least 60 minutes of physical activity daily and to minimize television viewing. B
Adults should engage in 30 to 90 minutes of moderate to vigorous intensity physical activity on most if not all days of the week. B

Consider bariatric surgery only in psychologically stable and motivated patients with BMI greater than 40 or BMI greater than 35 with significant comorbidities who have failed diet and lifestyle changes. C

Common preoperative screening studies include: electrocardiogram, polysomnogram, esophagogastroduodenoscopy, colonoscopy, right upper quadrant ultrasound. and appropriate laboratory work based on identified medical conditions (eg, electrolytes, blood sugar).

A systematic review found no difference in outcomes between routine or selectdive use of an upper GI series after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, and suggest that tachycardia and respiratory distress were the best early indicators of anastomotic leak.
A clinical decision rule has been developed and validated to predict mortality risk in patients undergoing bariatric surgery ().

Bariatric surgery is an option for patients with a BMI greater than 40 (or >35 with serious obesity-related comorbidity); failure of an integrated, nonsurgical weight loss program; and psychological stability with strong motivation toward postoperative lifestyle changes.

Morbidly obese patients are at risk for multiple medical conditions that may affect their risk for surgery. Good control of diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and congestive heart failure should be established preoperatively.
Bariatric surgical procedures can produce substantial weight loss (28 to >40 kg) in morbidly obese patients. B
Bariatric surgery is highly effective in treating obesity-related comorbidities including diabetes, hyperlipidemia, hypertension; it is associated with lower all-cause mortality as well. A

Risks of surgery include postoperative mortality of 1% and a serious complication rate of 10%. Due to the high complication rate, patients should undergo careful preoperative screening to ensure their candidacy for surgery. C
Patients who elect bariatric surgery can improve their individual outcome by choosing an experienced bariatric surgeon practicing at a high-volume medical center. C

Bariatric surgical procedures can produce substantial weight loss (28 to >40 kg) in morbidly obese patients. Bariatric surgery is highly effective in treating obesity-related comorbidities including diabetes, hyperlipidemia, hypertension, cardiovascular risk, and, possibly, obstructive sleep apnea. It is also associated with improved quality of life in patients with diabetes.

Based on population registry studies with over 1.5 million patients, bariatric surgery is associated with lower all-cause mortality and a lower risk of developing many subsequent obesity-related conditions. Since these investigators excluded randomized trials, the patients' health habits and other unmeasured factors might account for the findings.

A recent meta-analysis of 11 studies with 796 obese diabetic patients (BMI 30-52, mean follow up 2 years) concluded that patients undergoing bariatrics lost 26 kg more weight compared with those undergoing non-surgical obesity treatment, and were substantially more likely to have a higher remission rate for DM-II (OR 14.1, 95% CI 6.7-29.9); however, bariatric surgery was associated with a 15% rate of iron deficiency anemia and an 8% rate of reoperation.

Among 2458 patients with a mean BMI of 45.9, the type of surgical procedure predicted for the 3 year outcomes. Patients getting a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) experienced more twice as much weight loss, and a 2 to 2.5 higher likelihood of remission of diabetes, dyslipidemia and hypertension than those surgically treated with laparoscopic adjustable gastric banding (LAGB).

In an open label study of 60 patients, those randomized to bariatric surgery had a high rate of remission of T2DM at 2 years (75% undergoing gastric bypass and 95% undergoing biliopancreatic diversion), but these rates were only 37% and 63% at 5 years.

Data are conflicting on the outcome of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). In a metaanalysis, bariatric surgery did not eliminate OSA; although post-surgical patients had a significantly reduced apnea hypopnea index, the mean apnea hypopnea index was consistent with moderately severe OSA.

Bariatric surgery (Roux-en-Y gastric bypass) in obese (but not morbidly so) patients with hypertension results in normal blood pressure in 35% of patients without ongoing hypertension treatment. Another approximately 38% of patients were able to control their blood pressure with at least one less medication. However, 30% became vitamin B12 deficient, 17% required a cholecystectomy, and 14% developed hyperparathyroidism.

In a systematic review and metaanalysis including over 4,000 adult patients with diabetes, 78.1% of patients had complete resolution and 86.6% had improved or resolved diabetes after surgery. These responses were most pronounced following procedures associated with a greater percentage of excess body weight loss (biliopancreatic diversion/duodenal switch, followed by gastric bypass) and were maintained for 2 years or more.
Restrictive procedures () including adjustable and vertical gastric banding lead to an average of about 50% excess weight loss after 2 years.

Combined malabsorptive and restrictive procedures () including roux-en-Y gastric bypass, biliopancreatic diversion, and duodenal switch lead to an average of about 60% excess weight loss after 2 years. A Cochrane review found little high quality evidence regarding intra-gastric balloons.
Patients who elect bariatric surgery can improve their individual outcome by choosing an experienced bariatric surgeon practicing at a high-volume medical center.
A Cochrane review found no well designed clinical trials of bariatric surgery in patients with non-alcoholic steatohepatitis.

A trial randomized 272 adults undergoing bariatric surgery to rivaroxaban 10 mg once daily for either 7 or 28 days following surgery. There was no difference in thromboembolic or bleeding events between the 7 and 28 day groups.

A small randomized trial compared bariatric surgery with behavioral/medical therapy for 80 women with PCOS and oligo or amenorrhea. Women in the surgery group had significantly more spontaneous ovulations (incidence rate ratio 2.5, 95% CI 1.5 to 4.2) but fertility outcomes were not reported.
Preoperative psychological counseling to ensure emotional stability, commitment to lifestyle changes, and reasonable expectations of surgery is highly recommended.

Common complications of bariatric surgery include: small bowel obstruction, wound infection, cholelithiasis, vomiting, dysphagia, constipation, malnutrition, vitamin deficiency, Wernicke encephalopathy, and dumping syndrome ( and ).

A large Scandinavian registry study found that the overall risk of serious post-op complications was 3.4%, with increased risk among older patients, those undergoing additional procedures, and those converting to open surgery. The center where surgery was performed was also important, with more experienced centers having lower rates of complications.
Pulmonary embolism is the leading cause of death following bariatric surgery.
Together, the roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) and the adjustable gastric banding (AGB) have a postoperative mortality rate of 1% and a rate of serious complications of 10%.

The American Thoracic Society published a guideline on obesity-hypoventilation syndrome, but found only very low quality evidence. They recommend using serum bicarbonate levels to establish the diagnosis when clinical suspicion is <20%, and an ABG when >20%. CPAP is recommended for treatment.
Morbid obesity reduces an individual's life expectancy by 5 to 20 years. B
Bariatric surgery can reduce all-cause mortality by up to 40% in morbidly obese patients. B
Postoperative complications including abdominal pain and fever should be immediately evaluated. C
A clinical rule can predict the risk of perioperative mortality ().
Morbid obesity reduces an individual's life expectancy by 5 to 20 years.
Bariatric surgery patients generally lose weight for 2 years postoperatively followed by modest weight regain thereafter.
Patients undergoing restrictive procedures, including LapBand and vertical banded gastroplasty, generally sustain a weight loss of 13% to 16% of their initial weight at 10 years.
Patients undergoing RYGB sustain a weight loss of 25% of their initial weight at 10 years.

A Swedish study identified 2007 patients undergoing bariatric surgery and 2040 matched controls who received usual care for obesity, as well as 1135 persons from the general population. After 22 to 24 years of follow-up, all-cause mortality was lower in the surgery group (22.8% vs 26.4%, p < 0.001, NNT = 28). The likelihood of both cardiovascular and cancer death were lower. While the median life expectancy was 3 years longer in the surgery group, it was 5.5 years shorter than in the general population reference group.

A systematic review of 14 studies concluded, similar to the Cochrane review, that gastric bypass surgery results in greater weight loss and fewer long-term complications than banding; perioperative complications are higher and the surgery is more complicated. The authors caution that study quality is poor and only one trial was an RCT.

Two large observational studies found that bariatric surgery is associated with lower all-cause mortality. In one, morbidly obese patients undergoing bariatric surgery had a 40% reduction in all-cause mortality (38 vs. 57 deaths/1000 persons over 10 years). Cause-specific mortality reduction for gastric bypass includes 56% for coronary artery disease, 92% for diabetes mellitus, and 60% for cancer.
A systematic review found heterogeneous data regarding the impact of bariatric surgery on cancer risk.
Gastric bypass patients have a 52% increase in mortality from accidents and suicide postoperatively, perhaps secondary to undiagnosed psychopathology.

The comparative safety and long-term efficacy of different bariatric surgical procedures remains unclear. A recent metaanalysis found that weight loss favored bypass surgery over banding but attrition was extremely high at the furthest time point (>3 years) with only 82.6% of gastric banding and 89% of gastric bypass remaining available for follow-up assessment.
A clinical decision rule has been developed and validated to predict mortality risk in patients undergoing bariatric surgery ().
Promptly evaluate postoperative abdominal pain or fever to rule out obstruction, wound infection, or anastomotic leak.
Bariatric surgery patients require lifelong follow-up to ensure dietary and behavioral modification compliance.
Screen patients for nutritional deficiencies on a routine basis ().
Patients are at higher risk of osteoporosis due to sequestration of positively charged calcium ions from bone during weight loss.
Women of childbearing age should avoid pregnancy for at least 18 months following bariatric surgery.
A study of 79 women who became pregnant after gastric banding found no increase in maternal or fetal complications. The band was adjusted during pregnancy and mean weight gain was 9.6 kg.

In a critical review of pregnancy outcomes (case-control and cohort studies), authors found improved fertility and a reduced risk in obstetrical complications, particularly gestational diabetes, macrosomia and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, in women after operatively-induced weight loss vs. morbidly obese control groups of women. The incidence of intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), however, appears to be increased.

A second systematic review confirms improved maternal outcomes, including reduced risk of preeclampsia, compared with obese women without surgery and in one study comparing laparoscopic band surgery with obese control women, improved neonatal outcomes included lower rates of both macrosomia and low-birth weight.

The most recent systematic review of cohort studies confirmed that there are both benefits and harms with respect to pregnancy outcomes following bariatric surgery. Women undergoing surgery had fewer cesarean sections and were less likely to have a large for gestational age infant, but an increased risk for small for gestational infants and preterm deliveries. Benefits and harms were more strongly associated with malabsorptive surgeries than restrictive surgeries.

In a systematic review including 8 studies of laparoscopic adjustable gastric banding (LAGB) (N = 352) and 6 studies of Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) (N = 131) in children (mean age 16.8; range 9-21), both surgeries resulted in significant and sustained weight loss. While surgery appeared to resolve some cases of diabetes and hypertension, reported complications for LAGB were most frequent for band slippage and micronutrient deficiency and, for RYGB, more severe complications were documented including pulmonary embolism, shock, intestinal obstruction, postoperative bleeding, staple line leak, and severe malnutrition.
